thread.title: Apple's Snub Could Mean Qualcomm Stock Is a Bargain

title: Apple's Snub Could Mean Qualcomm Stock Is a Bargain
text:

https://www.barrons.com/articles/apples-snub-could-mean-qualcomm-stock-is-a-bargain-1541761200 Apple’s Snub Could Mean Qualcomm Stock Is a Bargain By Nov. 9, 2018 6:00 a.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Text size
Qualcomm (QCOM) is an outlier among the 5G patent licensers: Its stock is down year to date, despite all the hype surrounding the rollout of 5G wireless technology.
The stock’s problem is pretty simple to understand. Qualcomm and Apple (AAPL) are arguing over technology licensing fees. Apple stopped paying for the use of Qualcomm’s patent portfolio last year. That action trimmed roughly $2 billion of high-margin revenue off Qualcomm’s top line. (That’s about three days of revenue for Apple, for what it’s worth.)
The bad blood seems to be affecting Qualcomm’s modem business. Apple has started exclusively to use Intel ’s (INTC) 4G modems in its latest phones, even though Intel’s modem delivers slower speeds, at least according to Qualcomm.
Read more: Qualcomm Stock Plunges on Gloomy Outlook
Now the wireless world is abuzz over 5G technology, which can deliver up to one-gigabyte-per-second download speeds. That technology is rolling out in late 2019, and the transition adds to the drama between these two companies.
Qualcomm has patents that cover the manufacture of 5G products, just as it has in the 3G/4G arena. And it makes modems and antennae for 5G phones, just as it does for 3G/4G devices.
It isn’t clear what Apple will do as Qualcomm expands its agreements with its 300 or so licensees to cover use of its 5G patents. Apple is one of those firms with a 4G license, after all. It’s also not clear if Apple will sole-source 5G modems and shut out Qualcomm again. If Qualcomm’s speed claims are true, that may not be a prudent move for Apple.
It’s no wonder that Qualcomm stock is trading at a discount. Of course, every stock that is down a lot is at a “discount,” but Qualcomm is also at a discount to other patent licensers.
Nokia (NOK) and Ericsson (ERIC) are up over 30% and 50%, respectively, this year. And Nokia trades at 11.5 times 2021 earnings, while Ericsson trades at 15 times 2021 earnings. Qualcomm is trading at only 10.4 times 2021 earnings. (We picked 2021 to try to cut through today’s noise and capture some of the 5G business in estimates.)
If investors can stomach the volatility, then Qualcomm looks like the cheapest way to gain exposure to 5G trends.
A very large customer can endure more pain than a much smaller supplier—and the larger firm can leverage that position to extract some cost savings. A negotiated settlement may be in the cards.
